items.s: The option is in-the-money when the underlying stock trades above the strike price.
items.w: Remember call up, put down: calls are in-the-money when market value is above the strike price.

items.s: The buyer’s breakeven is the strike price minus the premium paid.
items.w: Put down means subtract the premium from the strike to find the breakeven, for long and short alike.

items.s: Buying one protects an investor who is short the underlying stock.
items.w: A purchased call locks in a fixed buying price, which caps the unlimited risk of a short sale.

items.s: Buying one protects an investor who owns the underlying stock against a falling market.
items.w: A protective put lets the owner sell at the strike no matter how low the stock falls.

items.s: An uncovered writer faces unlimited loss if the stock keeps rising.
items.w: A naked call writer must buy at any market price and deliver at the strike, so the loss is unlimited.

items.s: The writer is obligated to buy the stock at the strike price if the option is exercised.
items.w: A put writer is put the shares, meaning he must purchase them at the strike when the holder exercises.

items.s: The investor owns the stock and pays a premium for the option as downside insurance.
items.w: A protective put is a purchased option, so the investor pays a premium to hedge a long stock position.

items.s: The investor owns the stock and receives a premium, giving up gains above the strike.
items.w: A covered call writer collects premium income but loses profit when the stock trades above the strike.

items.s: Maximum gain is unlimited as the stock price continues to rise.
items.w: The put simply expires if the stock rises, so the stock’s appreciation is uncapped beyond the premium cost.

items.s: Maximum gain is limited to the premium plus strike price minus the stock’s cost basis.
items.w: Above the strike the call is exercised and the stock is called away, which caps the position’s gain.

items.s: Breakeven is the cost basis of the stock plus the premium paid.
items.w: The stock must rise enough to recover the premium paid for the put before the position shows a profit.

items.s: Breakeven is the stock purchase price minus the premium received.
items.w: The premium received cushions a decline, so the position breaks even below the original purchase price.

items.s: Exercise results in the actual purchase or sale of 100 shares of stock per contract.
items.w: Equity options have physical settlement, so shares change hands when the contract is exercised.

items.s: Exercise results in a cash payment of the index-to-strike difference times a multiplier, often $100.
items.w: Index options settle in cash because no securities change hands when the contract is exercised.

items.s: Its value derives from the closing value of a benchmark such as the S&P 500.
items.w: Index options are based on the closing index level rather than on the price of any one stock.

items.s: Its value is tied to the performance of one single underlying company’s stock.
items.w: Equity options derive value from a single stock, unlike index options that track a basket of stocks.

items.s: Buying a put on it is the best option-based hedge for an entire diversified portfolio.
items.w: An index put gains when the broad market falls, offsetting losses across a diversified stock portfolio.

items.s: The seller of the underlying must make good delivery of 100 shares when the option is exercised.
items.w: Equity option exercise requires delivery of shares, with the call seller or put buyer delivering the stock.

items.s: The buyer may exercise any time he chooses before the expiration date.
items.w: American-style contracts can be exercised any time the buyer chooses prior to the expiration date.

items.s: The buyer may exercise only on the expiration date itself.
items.w: European-style contracts allow exercise solely on the expiration date, never before it.

items.s: Most single stock options use this exercise style.
items.w: The book states that most single stock options are American-style, unlike many index options.

items.s: Stock index options are often this exercise style.
items.w: Index options are frequently European-style, so they are exercised only on the expiration date.

items.s: Options on the VIX volatility index use this exercise style.
items.w: The Knopman Note says VIX options have European-style exercises, meaning exercise only at expiration.

items.s: A call holder whose option goes deep in-the-money months before expiration may exercise right away.
items.w: Because exercise is allowed at any time before expiration, the holder controls timing across the contract’s life.

items.s: The amount by which an option is in-the-money.
items.w: Intrinsic value measures how far the option is in-the-money, and it is zero when out-of-the-money.

items.s: The entire premium of an out-of-the-money option consists of this component.
items.w: An out-of-the-money option has zero intrinsic value, so its whole premium is time value.

items.s: For a 60 call with the stock at $68, this component is $8.
items.w: A call’s intrinsic value is market value minus strike, which is $68 minus $60, or $8.

items.s: For a 60 call quoted at 9.50 with the stock at $68, this component is $1.50.
items.w: Time value is the premium less intrinsic value, so $9.50 minus the $8 intrinsic value is $1.50.

items.s: It reflects the remaining time to expiration and shrinks quickly in the final weeks.
items.w: Time value is highest with more time remaining and quickly declines as expiration approaches.

items.s: For an in-the-money put, it equals the strike price minus the stock price, and it is never negative.
items.w: A put’s intrinsic value is strike less market value, with a floor of zero for out-of-the-money puts.
